objectives: Identify neck stiffness and photophobia as meningitis danger signs in febrile illness.
Choose urgent stabilization and referral rather than routine outpatient fever treatment.
Avoid delays from low-yield tests when clinical red flags are already present.
takeaways: Neck stiffness plus fever should trigger emergency thinking at HC III.
Do not delay referral while waiting for routine outpatient investigations.
Early communication and documented pre-referral care improve safety.
learnCaseOverrides.blurb: A young man with fever cannot flex his neck and avoids light. Decide whether this is routine fever or a referral emergency.

sections.title: Chief complaint
sections.text: High fever, severe headache, neck pain, and photophobia

sections.title: Companion report
sections.text: Symptoms worsened overnight; he keeps eyes closed because light worsens headache.

coach.title: Moses appears acutely ill
coach.body: He lies still, avoids bright light, and reports severe headache with neck pain. Your first decision is triage urgency.
coach.quote: “Please switch off that light; my head is too painful.”

teach.label: Clinical framing
teach.text: Fever with meningeal features should be treated as potentially life-threatening until proven otherwise.

critical.title: Meningeal red flags
critical.body: Fever with neck stiffness and photophobia indicates high-risk CNS infection.

coach.title: What is your priority?
coach.body: Pick the action that aligns with these danger signs.

question.prompt: What is the best immediate plan?

options.text: Treat as suspected meningitis/severe febrile illness, stabilize, and arrange urgent referral
Manage as outpatient migraine and review after oral analgesics
Start oral AL only and reassess tomorrow
Wait for full laboratory panel before deciding referral

question.right: Correct. Fever 39.2 C with neck stiffness and photophobia is a danger-sign pattern that requires urgent referral-level management per Uganda Clinical Guidelines 2023.
question.wrong: This is not routine headache care. Neck stiffness with high fever and photophobia must be escalated urgently; delaying referral can lead to rapid deterioration.

coach.title: What should happen before transport?
coach.body: You have enough evidence to act now.

question.prompt: Which action is most appropriate now?

options.text: Give pre-referral empiric treatment per protocol and transfer urgently while monitoring airway and vitals
Delay all treatment until lumbar puncture is done at HC III
Because malaria RDT is negative, discharge with analgesics only
Observe for 12 hours to see if fever settles before referral

question.right: Correct. A negative malaria RDT does not remove meningitis risk. Uganda Clinical Guidelines 2023 support urgent referral with prompt pre-referral treatment for suspected severe CNS infection.
question.wrong: Waiting for additional outpatient procedures is unsafe in this pattern. Moses already has high-risk signs that require immediate escalation.

coach.title: How do you complete the transfer safely?
coach.body: Pick the handover approach that helps receiving clinicians act quickly.

question.prompt: What is the best handover action?

options.text: Call ahead and send a written note with vitals, red flags, and pre-referral care given
Send patient without documentation to avoid delaying departure
Record only final diagnosis and omit unstable observations
Keep patient until every possible cause is ruled out at HC III

question.right: Correct. Fast transfer plus high-quality handover shortens time to definitive care and reduces repeated assessment delays.
question.wrong: Poor referral communication can waste critical minutes. This case needs immediate, documented escalation.

sections.title: Case outcome
sections.text: You identified meningitis danger signs and prioritized emergency referral care.
sections.emphasis: Routine outpatient fever pathways were unsafe for this presentation.

coach.title: Key teaching points
coach.body: Moses had classic meningeal warning features on arrival: neck stiffness, photophobia, severe headache, and high fever. Uganda Clinical Guidelines 2023 support urgent stabilization, pre-referral treatment, and immediate transfer instead of watchful outpatient management.

teach.label: Clinician review
teach.text: When neurologic danger signs are present, avoid anchoring on common fever diagnoses and escalate early.
